name: Lavoisier’s oxygen chemistry
description: Lavoisier synthesized an oxygen-centered account of combustion and a quantitative chemical system.

impact.note: Replaced phlogiston with a quantitative chemistry of elements among chemists across Europe; nearly all later chemistry and the fields using it rest on it.

date.label: 5 September 1775 or 1777
date.basis: Two inspected English translations give conflicting reading years; both say the memoir was printed in 1780.

events.statement: Lavoisier presented a general combustion hypothesis identifying Priestley’s dephlogisticated air with pure air supporting combustion.
events.scope: The two translators disagree on the year of the Academy reading; this event is not a claim of first formulation.

evidence.supports: The translated memoir identifies Priestley’s dephlogisticated air with the pure air that supports combustion; the editor dates its Academy reading to 5 September 1777 and printing to 1780.
Another translated edition dates the reading 5 September 1775 and agrees on 1780 printing in the 1777 Academy volume.

contributions.resource: Authored the memoir presenting the combustion hypothesis.

earliest_record.rationale: The Academy presentation precedes the 1789 synthesis, but inspected translations disagree on its year.

caveats: Oxygen chemistry developed before the 1789 synthesis and depended on other researchers including Priestley. Lavoisier retained caloric and overgeneralized oxygen’s role in acids; the historic theory is not identical to modern chemistry. Two inspected English renderings date the memoir’s reading to 5 September 1775 and 1777 respectively; both date publication to 1780. The 1777 volume year is not the same as the print year.

research.note: Independent reading checked the source-supported event and chronology. Grain and other unreviewed facets remain provisional.
